Question:
Among the cars with an engine displacement of no less than 400 cubic millimeter, how many cars cost at least 30,000?

Evidence:
engine displacement of no less than 400 cubic millimeter refers to displacement > 400; cost at least 30,000 refers to price > 30000
answer: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM data AS T1 INNER JOIN price AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T1.displacement > 400 AND T2.price > 30000

metadata.question: Among the cars with an engine displacement of no less than 400 cubic millimeter, how many cars cost at least 30,000?
metadata.evidence: engine displacement of no less than 400 cubic millimeter refers to displacement > 400; cost at least 30,000 refers to price > 30000

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from `data`, where each car's engine displacement is stored: `FROM data AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join `price` on the shared car ID so each car is paired with its cost: `FROM data AS T1 INNER JOIN price AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the cars to those whose displacement is greater than 400: `FROM data AS T1 INNER JOIN price AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T1.displacement > 400`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I further restrict the matched cars to those priced above 30000: `FROM data AS T1 INNER JOIN price AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T1.displacement > 400 AND T2.price > 30000`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I count all cars satisfying both conditions: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM data AS T1 INNER JOIN price AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T1.displacement > 400 AND T2.price > 30000`.

What are the bonds that have phosphorus and nitrogen as their atom elements?

Question:
List all the pay rates of all employees that were hired at 20 years of age.

Evidence:
pay rate refers to Rate; 20 years old at the time of being hired refers to SUBTRACT(year(HireDate)), (year(BirthDate))) = 20;
answer: SELECT T2.Rate FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeePayHistory AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE STRFTIME('%Y', T1.HireDate) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.BirthDate) = 20

prefix_hints.sol_4: I project the matching pay-history rates from `T2`: `SELECT T2.Rate FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeePayHistory AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE STRFTIME('%Y', T1.HireDate) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.BirthDate) = 20`.

Question:

Evidence:
DIVIDE(COUNT(PATIENT when DESCRIPTION = 'Influenza seasonal injectable preservative free'), COUNT(PATIENT)) as percentage where strftime('%Y', 2017); English refers ethnicity = 'english';
answer: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T2.DESCRIPTION = 'Influenza seasonal injectable preservative free' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T1.patient), SUM(CASE WHEN T1.ethnicity = 'english' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM patients AS T1 INNER JOIN immunizations AS T2 ON T1.patient = T2.PATIENT WHERE strftime('%Y', T2.DATE) = '2017'

Question:
Which Production Technician has the highest pay rate?

Evidence:
highest pay rate refers to MAX(Rate);
answer: SELECT T1.BusinessEntityID FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeePayHistory AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.JobTitle LIKE 'Production Technician%' ORDER BY T2.Rate DESC LIMIT 1

metadata.question: Which Production Technician has the highest pay rate?
metadata.evidence: highest pay rate refers to MAX(Rate);

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with employees so I can identify each technician by BusinessEntityID and inspect their job title: `FROM Employee AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join each employee to their pay history on the shared BusinessEntityID so their rates are available: `FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeePayHistory AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I keep job titles beginning with Production Technician to include every technician level: `FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeePayHistory AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.JobTitle LIKE 'Production Technician%'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I sort the matching pay-history records by rate in descending order, placing the highest rate first: `FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeePayHistory AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.JobTitle LIKE 'Production Technician%' ORDER BY T2.Rate DESC`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I return the BusinessEntityID from that first record and limit the result to one technician: `SELECT T1.BusinessEntityID FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeePayHistory AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.JobTitle LIKE 'Production Technician%' ORDER BY T2.Rate DESC LIMIT 1`.

Question:
Find the id of students who do not have a cat pet.
answer: SELECT stuid FROM student EXCEPT SELECT T1.stuid FROM student AS T1 JOIN has_pet AS T2 ON T1.stuid  =  T2.stuid JOIN pets AS T3 ON T3.petid  =  T2.petid WHERE T3.pettype  =  'cat'

metadata.question: Find the id of students who do not have a cat pet.

intermediate_turns.question: How many students have a cat pet?
intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT count ( * )  FROM student AS T1 JOIN has_pet AS T2 ON T1.stuid  =  T2.stuid JOIN pets AS T3 ON T3.petid  =  T2.petid WHERE T3.pettype  =  'cat'

intermediate_turns.question: And what about students that don't have a cat pet?
intermediate_turns.sql: select count ( * )  from  ( SELECT stuid FROM student EXCEPT SELECT T1.stuid FROM student AS T1 JOIN has_pet AS T2 ON T1.stuid   =   T2.stuid JOIN pets AS T3 ON T3.petid   =   T2.petid WHERE T3.pettype   =   'cat' )

intermediate_turns.question: And what are their ids?
intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT stuid FROM student EXCEPT SELECT T1.stuid FROM student AS T1 JOIN has_pet AS T2 ON T1.stuid   =   T2.stuid JOIN pets AS T3 ON T3.petid   =   T2.petid WHERE T3.pettype   =   'cat'

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with the ids of all students as the full candidate set: `SELECT stuid FROM student`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I use EXCEPT to subtract the ids that will be associated with cat ownership: `SELECT stuid FROM student EXCEPT SELECT T1.stuid FROM student AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I join each student to their pet associations through the shared student id: `SELECT stuid FROM student EXCEPT SELECT T1.stuid FROM student AS T1 JOIN has_pet AS T2 ON T1.stuid = T2.stuid`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I continue from each association to the corresponding pet so its type is available: `SELECT stuid FROM student EXCEPT SELECT T1.stuid FROM student AS T1 JOIN has_pet AS T2 ON T1.stuid = T2.stuid JOIN pets AS T3 ON T3.petid = T2.petid`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I restrict the subtracted set to students whose associated pet is a cat, leaving the ids of students without a cat: `SELECT stuid FROM student EXCEPT SELECT T1.stuid FROM student AS T1 JOIN has_pet AS T2 ON T1.stuid = T2.stuid JOIN pets AS T3 ON T3.petid = T2.petid WHERE T3.pettype = 'cat'`.

Question:
Return the number of routes with destination airport in Italy operated by the airline with name 'American Airlines'.
answer: SELECT count(*) FROM routes AS T1 JOIN airports AS T2 ON T1.dst_apid  =  T2.apid JOIN airlines AS T3 ON T1.alid  =  T3.alid WHERE T2.country  =  'Italy' AND T3.name  =  'American Airlines'

metadata.question: Return the number of routes with destination airport in Italy operated by the airline with name 'American Airlines'.

intermediate_turns.question: how many routes are operated by the airline with name 'American Airlines'.
intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM routes AS T1 JOIN airlines AS T2 ON T1.alid  =  T2.alid WHERE T2.name  =  'American Airlines'

intermediate_turns.question: how many of them list the US as the destination?
intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM routes AS T1 JOIN airports AS T2 ON T1.dst_apid  =  T2.apid JOIN airlines AS T3 ON T1.alid  =  T3.alid WHERE T2.country  =  'United States' AND T3.name  =  'American Airlines'

intermediate_turns.question: how about for Italy?
intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM routes AS T1 JOIN airports AS T2 ON T1.dst_apid  =  T2.apid JOIN airlines AS T3 ON T1.alid  =  T3.alid WHERE T2.country  =  'Italy' AND T3.name  =  'American Airlines'

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from `routes` and join each route to its destination airport through `dst_apid`: `FROM routes AS T1 JOIN airports AS T2 ON T1.dst_apid  =  T2.apid`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I then join the operating airline through `alid` so its name is available: `FROM routes AS T1 JOIN airports AS T2 ON T1.dst_apid  =  T2.apid JOIN airlines AS T3 ON T1.alid  =  T3.alid`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the destination airports to those in Italy: `FROM routes AS T1 JOIN airports AS T2 ON T1.dst_apid  =  T2.apid JOIN airlines AS T3 ON T1.alid  =  T3.alid WHERE T2.country  =  'Italy'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I further restrict the routes to those operated by American Airlines: `FROM routes AS T1 JOIN airports AS T2 ON T1.dst_apid  =  T2.apid JOIN airlines AS T3 ON T1.alid  =  T3.alid WHERE T2.country  =  'Italy' AND T3.name  =  'American Airlines'`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I count all routes satisfying both conditions: `SELECT count(*) FROM routes AS T1 JOIN airports AS T2 ON T1.dst_apid  =  T2.apid JOIN airlines AS T3 ON T1.alid  =  T3.alid WHERE T2.country  =  'Italy' AND T3.name  =  'American Airlines'`.

prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I count the matching employee business entity ids: `SELECT COUNT(T1.BusinessEntityID) FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.Gender = 'M' AND T2.PersonType = 'SP'`.

metadata.question: What is the name and id of the staff who recorded the fault log but has not contacted any visiting engineers?

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with staff members who recorded fault-log entries by joining `Staff` to `Fault_Log` through the recording staff id: `FROM Staff AS T1 JOIN Fault_Log AS T2 ON T1.staff_id  =  T2.recorded_by_staff_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I project each recording staff member's name and id: `SELECT T1.staff_name ,  T1.staff_id FROM Staff AS T1 JOIN Fault_Log AS T2 ON T1.staff_id  =  T2.recorded_by_staff_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I use EXCEPT to remove staff members who appear as contacts for engineer visits: `SELECT T1.staff_name ,  T1.staff_id FROM Staff AS T1 JOIN Fault_Log AS T2 ON T1.staff_id  =  T2.recorded_by_staff_id EXCEPT`.

Question:
Between 2003 to 2005, what are the given names of the players with the most number of games played whose Penalty minutes is between 200 to 250?

Evidence:
penalty minutes refers to PIM; year of scoring BETWEEN 2003 AND 2005; most number of games played refers to max(GP)
answer: SELECT T2.nameGiven FROM Scoring AS T1 INNER JOIN Master AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID AND T1.PIM BETWEEN 200 AND 250 AND T1.year BETWEEN 2003 AND 2005 ORDER BY T1.GP DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.sol_2: I join `Master` by player id so I can retrieve each qualifying player's given name: `FROM Scoring AS T1 INNER JOIN Master AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I extend the join condition to keep scoring records with penalty minutes between 200 and 250: `FROM Scoring AS T1 INNER JOIN Master AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID AND T1.PIM BETWEEN 200 AND 250`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I also restrict the scoring years to 2003 through 2005, then sort games played from highest to lowest: `FROM Scoring AS T1 INNER JOIN Master AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID AND T1.PIM BETWEEN 200 AND 250 AND T1.year BETWEEN 2003 AND 2005 ORDER BY T1.GP DESC`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I project the given name and retain only the top-ranked player by games played: `SELECT T2.nameGiven FROM Scoring AS T1 INNER JOIN Master AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID AND T1.PIM BETWEEN 200 AND 250 AND T1.year BETWEEN 2003 AND 2005 ORDER BY T1.GP DESC LIMIT 1`.

How many letters are there in Catherine Ward's e-mail account passwords?

Evidence:
Catherine Ward refers to the name of BusinessEntityID; how many letters in password for the e-mail account refers to LENGTH(PasswordHash)
answer: SELECT LENGTH(T2.PasswordHash) FROM Person AS T1 INNER JOIN Password AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.FirstName = 'Catherine' AND T1.LastName = 'Ward'

metadata.question: How many games were sold on the DS platform on average in the 4 different regions?
metadata.evidence: on the DS platform refers to platform_name = 'DS'; number of games sold on average = divide(sum(multiply(num_sales, 100000)), 4) where platform_name = 'DS'

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from regional sales, where each recorded sales amount is stored: `FROM region_sales AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join each sales record to its game-platform release so I can reach the associated platform: `FROM region_sales AS T1 INNER JOIN game_platform AS T2 ON T1.game_platform_id = T2.id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I then join the platform table to make the platform name available: `FROM region_sales AS T1 INNER JOIN game_platform AS T2 ON T1.game_platform_id = T2.id INNER JOIN platform AS T3 ON T2.platform_id = T3.id`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I restrict the sales records to the DS platform: `FROM region_sales AS T1 INNER JOIN game_platform AS T2 ON T1.game_platform_id = T2.id INNER JOIN platform AS T3 ON T2.platform_id = T3.id WHERE T3.platform_name = 'DS'`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I sum DS sales, convert the values by multiplying by 100000, and divide by the four regions to obtain the regional average: `SELECT SUM(T1.num_sales) * 100000 / 4 FROM region_sales AS T1 INNER JOIN game_platform AS T2 ON T1.game_platform_id = T2.id INNER JOIN platform AS T3 ON T2.platform_id = T3.id WHERE T3.platform_name = 'DS'`.

Question:
Find the claims that led to more than two settlements or have the maximum claim value. For each of them, return the date the claim was made and the id of the claim.
answer: SELECT T1.Date_Claim_Made ,  T1.Claim_id FROM Claims AS T1 JOIN Settlements AS T2 ON T1.Claim_id  =  T2.Claim_id GROUP BY T1.Claim_id HAVING count(*)  >  2 UNION SELECT T1.Date_Claim_Made ,  T1.Claim_id FROM Claims AS T1 JOIN Settlements AS T2 ON T1.Claim_id  =  T2.Claim_id WHERE T1.Amount_Claimed  =  ( SELECT max(Amount_Claimed) FROM Claims )

metadata.question: Find the claims that led to more than two settlements or have the maximum claim value. For each of them, return the date the claim was made and the id of the claim.

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with claims joined to their settlements so I can count how many settlements each claim produced: `FROM Claims AS T1 JOIN Settlements AS T2 ON T1.Claim_id = T2.Claim_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I group the joined rows by claim and retain claims associated with more than two settlement rows: `FROM Claims AS T1 JOIN Settlements AS T2 ON T1.Claim_id = T2.Claim_id GROUP BY T1.Claim_id HAVING count(*) > 2`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I project the claim date and claim id for this first set of qualifying claims: `SELECT T1.Date_Claim_Made, T1.Claim_id FROM Claims AS T1 JOIN Settlements AS T2 ON T1.Claim_id = T2.Claim_id GROUP BY T1.Claim_id HAVING count(*) > 2`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I add a UNION branch that joins the same tables for claims qualifying by their claimed amount: `SELECT T1.Date_Claim_Made, T1.Claim_id FROM Claims AS T1 JOIN Settlements AS T2 ON T1.Claim_id = T2.Claim_id GROUP BY T1.Claim_id HAVING count(*) > 2 UNION SELECT T1.Date_Claim_Made, T1.Claim_id FROM Claims AS T1 JOIN Settlements AS T2 ON T1.Claim_id = T2.Claim_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I finish the second branch by comparing each claim's value with the maximum Amount_Claimed across all claims: `SELECT T1.Date_Claim_Made ,  T1.Claim_id FROM Claims AS T1 JOIN Settlements AS T2 ON T1.Claim_id  =  T2.Claim_id GROUP BY T1.Claim_id HAVING count(*)  >  2 UNION SELECT T1.Date_Claim_Made ,  T1.Claim_id FROM Claims AS T1 JOIN Settlements AS T2 ON T1.Claim_id  =  T2.Claim_id WHERE T1.Amount_Claimed  =  ( SELECT max(Amount_Claimed) FROM Claims )`.

prefix_hints.sol_3: I sort the matched target users by trust score in ascending order so the lowest score comes first: `SELECT T1.name FROM useracct AS T1 JOIN trust AS T2 ON T1.u_id  =  T2.target_u_id ORDER BY trust`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I retain only the first row, which identifies the target user with the lowest trust score: `SELECT T1.name FROM useracct AS T1 JOIN trust AS T2 ON T1.u_id  =  T2.target_u_id ORDER BY trust LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: This completes the query: `SELECT T1.name FROM useracct AS T1 JOIN trust AS T2 ON T1.u_id  =  T2.target_u_id ORDER BY trust LIMIT 1`.

Question:
When did the first-through-twelfth-grade school with the largest enrollment open?

Evidence:
K-12 means First-through-twelfth-grade
answer: SELECT T2.OpenDate FROM frpm AS T1 INNER JOIN schools AS T2 ON T1.CDSCode = T2.CDSCode ORDER BY T1.`Enrollment (K-12)` DESC LIMIT 1

Question:
Calculate the total quantity ordered for 18th Century Vintage Horse Carriage and the average price.

Evidence:
18th Century Vintage Horse Carriage is a product name; average price = AVG(priceEach);
answer: SELECT SUM(T2.quantityOrdered) , SUM(T2.quantityOrdered * T2.priceEach) / SUM(T2.quantityOrdered) FROM products AS T1 INNER JOIN orderdetails AS T2 ON T1.productCode = T2.productCode WHERE T1.productName = '18th Century Vintage Horse Carriage'

prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the joined rows to the 18th Century Vintage Horse Carriage: `FROM products AS T1 INNER JOIN orderdetails AS T2 ON T1.productCode = T2.productCode WHERE T1.productName = '18th Century Vintage Horse Carriage'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I sum `quantityOrdered` to calculate the product's total ordered quantity: `SELECT SUM(T2.quantityOrdered) FROM products AS T1 INNER JOIN orderdetails AS T2 ON T1.productCode = T2.productCode WHERE T1.productName = '18th Century Vintage Horse Carriage'`.

Question:
What are the album titles for albums containing both 'Reggae' and 'Rock' genre tracks?
answer: SELECT T1.Title FROM Album AS T1 JOIN Track AS T2 ON T1.AlbumId  =  T2.AlbumId JOIN Genre AS T3 ON T2.GenreID  =  T3.GenreID WHERE T3.Name  =  'Reggae' INTERSECT SELECT T1.Title FROM Album AS T1 JOIN Track AS T2 ON T1.AlbumId  =  T2.AlbumId JOIN Genre AS T3 ON T2.GenreID  =  T3.GenreID WHERE T3.Name  =  'Rock'

prefix_hints.sol_3: I project the album titles whose joined tracks have the Reggae genre: `SELECT T1.Title FROM Album AS T1 JOIN Track AS T2 ON T1.AlbumId  =  T2.AlbumId JOIN Genre AS T3 ON T2.GenreID  =  T3.GenreID WHERE T3.Name  =  'Reggae'`.

answer: SELECT MIN(T1.DOB) FROM Player AS T1 INNER JOIN Bowling_Style AS T2 ON T1.Bowling_skill = T2.Bowling_Id WHERE T2.Bowling_Skill = 'Legbreak'

Question:
What are first and last names of players participating in all star game in 1998?
answer: SELECT name_first ,  name_last FROM player AS T1 JOIN all_star AS T2 ON T1.player_id  =  T2.player_id WHERE YEAR  =  1998

intermediate_turns.question: in addition to Rick Ferrell, Lefty Gomez, and player ID gehrilo01, can you tell me the first and last names of the other players participating in 1998 all star game?

Question:
For each end station id, what is its name, latitude, and minimum duration for trips ended there?
answer: SELECT T1.name ,  T1.lat ,  min(T2.duration) FROM station AS T1 JOIN trip AS T2 ON T1.id  =  T2.end_station_id GROUP BY T2.end_station_id

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from `station` so each ending station's name and latitude are available: `FROM station AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join `trip` by matching the station id to each trip's end station id, which also makes trip duration available: `FROM station AS T1 JOIN trip AS T2 ON T1.id  =  T2.end_station_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I group the matched trips by end station id so the minimum duration is calculated separately for each station: `FROM station AS T1 JOIN trip AS T2 ON T1.id  =  T2.end_station_id GROUP BY T2.end_station_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I project the station name and latitude along with the minimum trip duration for each group: `SELECT T1.name ,  T1.lat ,  min(T2.duration) FROM station AS T1 JOIN trip AS T2 ON T1.id  =  T2.end_station_id GROUP BY T2.end_station_id`.

List all staff in the Shipping and Receiving department who are hired in 2009.

hired in 2009 refers to year(HireDate) = 2009

Question:
What is the highest lake area coverage of a country?

Evidence:
Lake area coverage = [sum(area of the lakes in the country) / (area of the country)] * 100%
answer: SELECT T2.Area * 100  / T3.Area FROM located AS T1 INNER JOIN lake AS T2 ON T1.Lake = T2.Name INNER JOIN country AS T3 ON T3.Code = T1.Country ORDER BY T2.Longitude DESC LIMIT 1

Question:
Find the net profit of the floral products which were delivered in 2021.

Evidence:
floral product refers to Product Name = 'Floral'; total net profit = SUM(Subtract(Unit Price, Unit Cost)); delivered in 2021 refers to DeliveryDate LIKE '%/21'

Question:
List the name of staff who has been assigned multiple jobs.
answer: SELECT T1.staff_name FROM staff AS T1 JOIN staff_department_assignments AS T2 ON T1.staff_id  =  T2.staff_id GROUP BY T2.staff_id HAVING COUNT (*)  >  1

metadata.question: List the name of staff who has been assigned multiple jobs.

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from `staff`, where each staff member’s name and id are stored: `FROM staff AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join the assignment records on staff id so each row represents one job assignment for a staff member: `FROM staff AS T1 JOIN staff_department_assignments AS T2 ON T1.staff_id  =  T2.staff_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I group the assignment rows by staff id so I can count each staff member’s jobs: `FROM staff AS T1 JOIN staff_department_assignments AS T2 ON T1.staff_id  =  T2.staff_id GROUP BY T2.staff_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I retain staff members whose assignment count is greater than one: `FROM staff AS T1 JOIN staff_department_assignments AS T2 ON T1.staff_id  =  T2.staff_id GROUP BY T2.staff_id HAVING COUNT (*)  >  1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I project the names of those staff members, completing the query: `SELECT T1.staff_name FROM staff AS T1 JOIN staff_department_assignments AS T2 ON T1.staff_id  =  T2.staff_id GROUP BY T2.staff_id HAVING COUNT (*)  >  1`.

Question:
what is the most populated capital in the usa
answer: SELECT city_name FROM city WHERE population  =  ( SELECT MAX ( t1.population ) FROM state AS t2 JOIN city AS t1 ON t2.capital  =  t1.city_name );

metadata.question: what is the most populated capital in the usa

prefix_hints.sol_1: I link each state to its capital's city record through the capital and city-name columns: `FROM state AS t2 JOIN city AS t1 ON t2.capital = t1.city_name`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I take the maximum population among those capital-city records: `SELECT MAX ( t1.population ) FROM state AS t2 JOIN city AS t1 ON t2.capital = t1.city_name`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I use that maximum as a scalar subquery and retain the city whose population equals it: `FROM city WHERE population = ( SELECT MAX ( t1.population ) FROM state AS t2 JOIN city AS t1 ON t2.capital = t1.city_name )`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I project the name of the matching city: `SELECT city_name FROM city WHERE population = ( SELECT MAX ( t1.population ) FROM state AS t2 JOIN city AS t1 ON t2.capital = t1.city_name )`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: This completes the query for the most populated capital: `SELECT city_name FROM city WHERE population  =  ( SELECT MAX ( t1.population ) FROM state AS t2 JOIN city AS t1 ON t2.capital  =  t1.city_name );`.

Question:
Which geographic area does the city with the second lowest tax rate belongs to? Indicate the name of the state or province as well.

Evidence:
geographic area to which the city belong refers to Group;
answer: SELECT T3.'Group', T2.Name FROM SalesTaxRate AS T1 INNER JOIN StateProvince AS T2 ON T1.StateProvinceID = T2.StateProvinceID INNER JOIN SalesTerritory AS T3 ON T2.TerritoryID = T3.TerritoryID ORDER BY T1.TaxRate LIMIT 1, 1

prefix_hints.sol_3: I sort the joined records by tax rate from lowest to highest: `FROM SalesTaxRate AS T1 INNER JOIN StateProvince AS T2 ON T1.StateProvinceID = T2.StateProvinceID INNER JOIN SalesTerritory AS T3 ON T2.TerritoryID = T3.TerritoryID ORDER BY T1.TaxRate`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I skip the lowest-tax record and retain the next one to obtain the second lowest tax rate: `FROM SalesTaxRate AS T1 INNER JOIN StateProvince AS T2 ON T1.StateProvinceID = T2.StateProvinceID INNER JOIN SalesTerritory AS T3 ON T2.TerritoryID = T3.TerritoryID ORDER BY T1.TaxRate LIMIT 1, 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I return that record's geographic group and state or province name: `SELECT T3.'Group', T2.Name FROM SalesTaxRate AS T1 INNER JOIN StateProvince AS T2 ON T1.StateProvinceID = T2.StateProvinceID INNER JOIN SalesTerritory AS T3 ON T2.TerritoryID = T3.TerritoryID ORDER BY T1.TaxRate LIMIT 1, 1`.

Question:
Which religion is most prevalent in Asia?

Evidence:
Most prevalent religion refers to the religion with the most population percentage
answer: SELECT T4.Name FROM continent AS T1 INNER JOIN encompasses AS T2 ON T1.Name = T2.Continent INNER JOIN country AS T3 ON T3.Code = T2.Country INNER JOIN religion AS T4 ON T4.Country = T3.Code WHERE T1.Name = 'Asia' GROUP BY T4.Name ORDER BY SUM(T4.Percentage) DESC LIMIT 1

metadata.question: Which religion is most prevalent in Asia?
metadata.evidence: Most prevalent religion refers to the religion with the most population percentage

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from continents and link Asia to the countries it encompasses: `FROM continent AS T1 INNER JOIN encompasses AS T2 ON T1.Name = T2.Continent INNER JOIN country AS T3 ON T3.Code = T2.Country`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join each country to its recorded religions so their population percentages are available: `FROM continent AS T1 INNER JOIN encompasses AS T2 ON T1.Name = T2.Continent INNER JOIN country AS T3 ON T3.Code = T2.Country INNER JOIN religion AS T4 ON T4.Country = T3.Code`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the joined records to the Asian continent and group them by religion name: `FROM continent AS T1 INNER JOIN encompasses AS T2 ON T1.Name = T2.Continent INNER JOIN country AS T3 ON T3.Code = T2.Country INNER JOIN religion AS T4 ON T4.Country = T3.Code WHERE T1.Name = 'Asia' GROUP BY T4.Name`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I rank the religions by their summed population percentages in descending order and retain the highest one: `FROM continent AS T1 INNER JOIN encompasses AS T2 ON T1.Name = T2.Continent INNER JOIN country AS T3 ON T3.Code = T2.Country INNER JOIN religion AS T4 ON T4.Country = T3.Code WHERE T1.Name = 'Asia' GROUP BY T4.Name ORDER BY SUM(T4.Percentage) DESC LIMIT 1`.

winning percentage refers to DIVIDE(w,g)*100; team DET refers to tmID = 'DET'

prefix_hints.sol_3: I sort the joined rows by the high estimate in descending order so the largest value comes first: `FROM film AS T1 JOIN film_market_estimation AS T2  ON T1.Film_ID  =  T2.Film_ID ORDER BY high_estimate DESC`.

Question:

answer: SELECT count(*) ,  T1.year FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T2.name  =  'Boston Red Stockings' GROUP BY T1.year

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from postseason records because each row identifies the winning team and year: `FROM postseason AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join the historical team records by matching the postseason winner to the team's Baseball-Reference identifier: `FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner  =  T2.team_id_br`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the joined records to the Boston Red Stockings: `FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T2.name  =  'Boston Red Stockings'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I group the qualifying postseason records by year so the wins can be counted separately for each year: `FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T2.name  =  'Boston Red Stockings' GROUP BY T1.year`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I count the winning postseason records in each group and return that count with its year: `SELECT count(*) ,  T1.year FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T2.name  =  'Boston Red Stockings' GROUP BY T1.year`.

Question:
How many employees with a pay rate of over 35 have more than 10 sick leave hours?

Evidence:
more than 10 sick leave hours refers to SickLeaveHours>10; pay rate over 35 refers to Rate>35;
answer: SELECT COUNT(T1.BusinessEntityID) FROM EmployeePayHistory AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T2.SickLeaveHours > 10 AND T1.Rate > 35

prefix_hints.sol_4: I further restrict the matched pay records to rates over 35: `FROM EmployeePayHistory AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T2.SickLeaveHours > 10 AND T1.Rate > 35`.

Question:
List out the user who is an elite user for consecutively 5 years or more and what is the user average star? How many likes does this user gets?

Evidence:
elite user for consecutively 5 years or more refers to user_id COUNT(year_id) > 5; Average star = AVG(likes)
answer: SELECT T2.user_average_stars, COUNT(T3.likes) FROM Elite AS T1 INNER JOIN Users AS T2 ON T1.user_id = T2.user_id INNER JOIN Tips AS T3 ON T3.user_id = T2.user_id GROUP BY T1.user_id HAVING COUNT(T1.user_id) > 5

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from the elite-year records so I can count each user's elite appearances: `FROM Elite AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join the user profile data to obtain each elite user's average-star value: `FROM Elite AS T1 INNER JOIN Users AS T2 ON T1.user_id = T2.user_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I then join the user's tips so their likes can be counted: `FROM Elite AS T1 INNER JOIN Users AS T2 ON T1.user_id = T2.user_id INNER JOIN Tips AS T3 ON T3.user_id = T2.user_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I group the joined records by user and retain users with more than five elite records: `FROM Elite AS T1 INNER JOIN Users AS T2 ON T1.user_id = T2.user_id INNER JOIN Tips AS T3 ON T3.user_id = T2.user_id GROUP BY T1.user_id HAVING COUNT(T1.user_id) > 5`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I return each qualifying user's average-star value and the count of their tip likes: `SELECT T2.user_average_stars, COUNT(T3.likes) FROM Elite AS T1 INNER JOIN Users AS T2 ON T1.user_id = T2.user_id INNER JOIN Tips AS T3 ON T3.user_id = T2.user_id GROUP BY T1.user_id HAVING COUNT(T1.user_id) > 5`.

has been yelping since 2004 refers to user_yelping_since_year = 2004
answer: SELECT DISTINCT T2.user_id FROM Users AS T1 INNER JOIN Elite AS T2 ON T1.user_id = T2.user_id WHERE T1.user_yelping_since_year = 2004

prefix_hints.sol_2: I join `Elite` on the user id so the result includes only users who are Yelp Elite members: `FROM Users AS T1 INNER JOIN Elite AS T2 ON T1.user_id = T2.user_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the users to those who have been yelping since 2004: `FROM Users AS T1 INNER JOIN Elite AS T2 ON T1.user_id = T2.user_id WHERE T1.user_yelping_since_year = 2004`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I project the Elite user id with `DISTINCT`, since a user can have Elite records for multiple years: `SELECT DISTINCT T2.user_id FROM Users AS T1 INNER JOIN Elite AS T2 ON T1.user_id = T2.user_id WHERE T1.user_yelping_since_year = 2004`.

Find the names of Japanese constructors that have once earned more than 5 points?
answer: SELECT T1.name FROM constructors AS T1 JOIN constructorstandings AS T2 ON T1.constructorid = T2.constructorid WHERE T1.nationality = "Japanese" AND T2.points > 5

metadata.question: Find the names of Japanese constructors that have once earned more than 5 points?

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with constructors so I can retrieve each constructor's name and nationality: `FROM constructors AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join the standings records where constructor points are stored, matching on constructorid: `FROM constructors AS T1 JOIN constructorstandings AS T2 ON T1.constructorid = T2.constructorid`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the joined rows to constructors whose nationality is Japanese: `FROM constructors AS T1 JOIN constructorstandings AS T2 ON T1.constructorid = T2.constructorid WHERE T1.nationality = "Japanese"`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I then require a standings record with more than 5 points, capturing constructors that have earned that amount at least once: `FROM constructors AS T1 JOIN constructorstandings AS T2 ON T1.constructorid = T2.constructorid WHERE T1.nationality = "Japanese" AND T2.points > 5`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I return the names of the matching constructors: `SELECT T1.name FROM constructors AS T1 JOIN constructorstandings AS T2 ON T1.constructorid = T2.constructorid WHERE T1.nationality = "Japanese" AND T2.points > 5`.

Question:
On what year did the youngest driver had his first qualifying race? Also state the name, date and time of the race.

Evidence:
date of birth refers to drivers.dob; The larger the birthday value, the younger the person is, and vice versa; first qualifying race refers to MIN(races.date);
answer: SELECT T3.year, T3.name, T3.date, T3.time FROM qualifying AS T1 INNER JOIN drivers AS T2 on T1.driverId = T2.driverId INNER JOIN races AS T3 on T1.raceId = T3.raceId WHERE T1.driverId = ( SELECT driverId FROM drivers ORDER BY dob DESC LIMIT 1 ) ORDER BY T3.date ASC LIMIT 1

Question:
How many goals were scored while the goalkeeper was on the ice in the 1924 WCHL by the goalie with the most goals scored?

Evidence:
WCHL is the league's abbreviated name which refers to lgID = 'WCHL'; most goals scored referst to MAX(PostGA); GA is abbreviation for Post Against which means number of goals recorded while the goalie is on the ice. Include all goals against during regulation and overtime play.
answer: SELECT SUM(PostGA) FROM Goalies WHERE lgID = 'WCHL' AND year = '1924' GROUP BY playerID ORDER BY SUM(PostGA) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.sol_4: I group the records by goalie and rank the summed `PostGA` values from highest to lowest: `FROM Goalies WHERE lgID = 'WCHL' AND year = '1924' GROUP BY playerID ORDER BY SUM(PostGA) DESC`.

metadata.question: What is the name of the publisher that released the most video games in 2007?
metadata.evidence: name of the publisher refers to publisher_name; publisher that released the most video games in 2007 refers to MAX(COUNT(publisher_name)) WHERE release_year = 2007;

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with the 2007 release records and link each platform release to its game-publisher association: `FROM game_platform AS T1 INNER JOIN game_publisher AS T2 ON T1.game_publisher_id = T2.id`.

prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the releases to the year 2007: `FROM game_platform AS T1 INNER JOIN game_publisher AS T2 ON T1.game_publisher_id = T2.id INNER JOIN publisher AS T3 ON T2.publisher_id = T3.id WHERE T1.release_year = 2007`.

Question:
What are the order dates of orders with price higher than 1000?
answer: SELECT T1.Order_Date FROM Customer_Orders AS T1 JOIN ORDER_ITEMS AS T2 ON T1.Order_ID  =  T2.Order_ID JOIN Products AS T3 ON T2.Product_ID  =  T3.Product_ID WHERE T3.Product_price  >  1000

metadata.question: What are the order dates of orders with price higher than 1000?

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from customer orders because they contain the requested order dates: `FROM Customer_Orders AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I link each order to its items through the shared order ID: `FROM Customer_Orders AS T1 JOIN ORDER_ITEMS AS T2 ON T1.Order_ID  =  T2.Order_ID`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I then join the items to their products so the corresponding product prices are available: `FROM Customer_Orders AS T1 JOIN ORDER_ITEMS AS T2 ON T1.Order_ID  =  T2.Order_ID JOIN Products AS T3 ON T2.Product_ID  =  T3.Product_ID`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I restrict the results to products whose price is higher than 1000: `FROM Customer_Orders AS T1 JOIN ORDER_ITEMS AS T2 ON T1.Order_ID  =  T2.Order_ID JOIN Products AS T3 ON T2.Product_ID  =  T3.Product_ID WHERE T3.Product_price  >  1000`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I return the order dates for the qualifying orders: `SELECT T1.Order_Date FROM Customer_Orders AS T1 JOIN ORDER_ITEMS AS T2 ON T1.Order_ID  =  T2.Order_ID JOIN Products AS T3 ON T2.Product_ID  =  T3.Product_ID WHERE T3.Product_price  >  1000`.

answer: SELECT T2.genre FROM movies AS T1 INNER JOIN movies2directors AS T2 ON T1.movieid = T2.movieid WHERE T1.isEnglish = 'F' GROUP BY T2.genre ORDER BY COUNT(T1.movieid) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.sol_2: I keep the non-English films identified by `isEnglish = 'F'`: `FROM movies AS T1 INNER JOIN movies2directors AS T2 ON T1.movieid = T2.movieid WHERE T1.isEnglish = 'F'`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I group the matching films by genre so each genre's films can be counted: `FROM movies AS T1 INNER JOIN movies2directors AS T2 ON T1.movieid = T2.movieid WHERE T1.isEnglish = 'F' GROUP BY T2.genre`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I sort the genre groups by their movie counts in descending order, placing the largest count first: `FROM movies AS T1 INNER JOIN movies2directors AS T2 ON T1.movieid = T2.movieid WHERE T1.isEnglish = 'F' GROUP BY T2.genre ORDER BY COUNT(T1.movieid) DESC`.

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with `country` and link each country to its recorded mountains through the country code: `FROM country AS T1 INNER JOIN geo_mountain AS T2 ON T1.Code = T2.Country`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join the mountain details so I can inspect each mountain's type and height: `FROM country AS T1 INNER JOIN geo_mountain AS T2 ON T1.Code = T2.Country INNER JOIN mountain AS T3 ON T3.Name = T2.Mountain`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the joined mountains to volcanoes: `FROM country AS T1 INNER JOIN geo_mountain AS T2 ON T1.Code = T2.Country INNER JOIN mountain AS T3 ON T3.Name = T2.Mountain WHERE T3.Type = 'volcano'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I sort the volcanoes from highest to lowest and retain the highest one: `FROM country AS T1 INNER JOIN geo_mountain AS T2 ON T1.Code = T2.Country INNER JOIN mountain AS T3 ON T3.Name = T2.Mountain WHERE T3.Type = 'volcano' ORDER BY T3.Height DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I project the province associated with that highest volcano, completing the query: `SELECT T1.Province FROM country AS T1 INNER JOIN geo_mountain AS T2 ON T1.Code = T2.Country INNER JOIN mountain AS T3 ON T3.Name = T2.Mountain WHERE T3.Type = 'volcano' ORDER BY T3.Height DESC LIMIT 1`.

Question:
What is the full name of the employee who has the most customers?
answer: SELECT T1.first_name , T1.last_name FROM employees AS T1 JOIN customers AS T2 ON T1.id  =  T2.support_rep_id GROUP BY T1.id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1

metadata.question: What is the full name of the employee who has the most customers?

prefix_hints.sol_1: I link each employee to the customers assigned to them through the support representative id: `FROM employees AS T1 JOIN customers AS T2 ON T1.id  =  T2.support_rep_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I group the joined rows by employee so each group represents that employee's customers: `FROM employees AS T1 JOIN customers AS T2 ON T1.id  =  T2.support_rep_id GROUP BY T1.id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I sort the employee groups by their customer counts in descending order, placing the employee with the most customers first: `FROM employees AS T1 JOIN customers AS T2 ON T1.id  =  T2.support_rep_id GROUP BY T1.id ORDER BY count(*) DESC`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I retain only the first employee from that ranking: `FROM employees AS T1 JOIN customers AS T2 ON T1.id  =  T2.support_rep_id GROUP BY T1.id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I project that employee's first and last names to complete the query: `SELECT T1.first_name , T1.last_name FROM employees AS T1 JOIN customers AS T2 ON T1.id  =  T2.support_rep_id GROUP BY T1.id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.

prefix_hints.sol_2: I link each actor to the movies they starred in through the cast mapping: `FROM actors AS T1 INNER JOIN movies2actors AS T2 ON T1.actorid = T2.actorid`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I then join those movies to their user ratings by movie id: `FROM actors AS T1 INNER JOIN movies2actors AS T2 ON T1.actorid = T2.actorid INNER JOIN u2base AS T3 ON T2.movieid = T3.movieid`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I keep the best actors with quality 5 and the matching movie ratings equal to 5: `FROM actors AS T1 INNER JOIN movies2actors AS T2 ON T1.actorid = T2.actorid INNER JOIN u2base AS T3 ON T2.movieid = T3.movieid WHERE T1.a_quality = 5 AND T3.rating = 5`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I count the actor ids among the qualifying joined rows: `SELECT COUNT(T1.actorid) FROM actors AS T1 INNER JOIN movies2actors AS T2 ON T1.actorid = T2.actorid INNER JOIN u2base AS T3 ON T2.movieid = T3.movieid WHERE T1.a_quality = 5 AND T3.rating = 5`.

Question:
Calculate the average length of employment for employee working in the Research and Development deparment.

Evidence:
average length of employment = AVG(subtract(2022, year(HireDate)))
answer: SELECT AVG(STRFTIME('%Y', CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.HireDate)) FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeeDepartmentHistory AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID INNER JOIN Department AS T3 ON T2.DepartmentID = T3.DepartmentID WHERE T3.Name = 'Research and Development'

Question:
What is the difference in salary of the top 2 employees with the highest number of territories in charge?

Evidence:
highest number of territories refers to max(TerritoryID); difference in salary = subtract(employeeA.Salary, employeeB.Salary)
answer: SELECT MAX(Salary) - MIN(Salary) FROM ( SELECT T1.Salary FROM Employees AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeeTerritories AS T2 ON T1.EmployeeID = T2.EmployeeID GROUP BY T1.EmployeeID, T1.Salary ORDER BY COUNT(T2.TerritoryID) DESC LIMIT 2 ) T1

intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT T1.response_received_date FROM Documents AS T1 JOIN Grants AS T2 ON T1.grant_id   =   T2.grant_id WHERE T2.grant_amount  >  100

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with documents and join their type records so the document descriptions are available: `FROM Documents AS T1 JOIN Document_Types AS T2 ON T1.document_type_code  =  T2.document_type_code`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I also join each document to its grant so I can test the grant amount: `FROM Documents AS T1 JOIN Document_Types AS T2 ON T1.document_type_code  =  T2.document_type_code JOIN Grants AS T3 ON T1.grant_id  =  T3.grant_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I first include documents whose type description is Regular: `FROM Documents AS T1 JOIN Document_Types AS T2 ON T1.document_type_code  =  T2.document_type_code JOIN Grants AS T3 ON T1.grant_id  =  T3.grant_id WHERE T2.document_description  =  'Regular'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I broaden the condition with OR to also include documents granted more than 100: `FROM Documents AS T1 JOIN Document_Types AS T2 ON T1.document_type_code  =  T2.document_type_code JOIN Grants AS T3 ON T1.grant_id  =  T3.grant_id WHERE T2.document_description  =  'Regular' OR T3.grant_amount  >  100`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I return the response received date for every matching document: `SELECT T1.response_received_date FROM Documents AS T1 JOIN Document_Types AS T2 ON T1.document_type_code  =  T2.document_type_code JOIN Grants AS T3 ON T1.grant_id  =  T3.grant_id WHERE T2.document_description  =  'Regular' OR T3.grant_amount  >  100`.

Question:
What is the product with the most profit?

Evidence:
profit = SUBTRACT(ListPrice, StandardCost);
answer: SELECT T1.ProductID FROM ProductListPriceHistory AS T1 INNER JOIN ProductCostHistory AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID ORDER BY T1.ListPrice - T2.StandardCost DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.sol_3: I calculate profit as ListPrice minus StandardCost and sort from highest profit to lowest: `FROM ProductListPriceHistory AS T1 INNER JOIN ProductCostHistory AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID ORDER BY T1.ListPrice - T2.StandardCost DESC`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I retain only the first row in that descending profit order: `FROM ProductListPriceHistory AS T1 INNER JOIN ProductCostHistory AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID ORDER BY T1.ListPrice - T2.StandardCost DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I return the ProductID from the highest-profit row: `SELECT T1.ProductID FROM ProductListPriceHistory AS T1 INNER JOIN ProductCostHistory AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID ORDER BY T1.ListPrice - T2.StandardCost DESC LIMIT 1`.

Question:
What is the average body mass index for patients with higher total cholesterol?

Evidence:
average body mass index = DIVIDE(SUM(observations.VALUE), COUNT(PATIENT) WHERE observations.DESCRIPTION = 'Body Mass Index'); body mass index refers to observations.DESCRIPTION = 'Body Mass Index'; higher total cholesterol refers to observations.DESCRIPTION = 'Total Cholesterol' and observations.VALUE > = 200;
answer: SELECT SUM(T1.VALUE) / COUNT(T1.PATIENT) FROM observations AS T1 INNER JOIN ( SELECT DISTINCT PATIENT FROM observations WHERE DESCRIPTION = 'Total Cholesterol' AND VALUE > 200 ) AS T2 ON T1.PATIENT = T2.PATIENT WHERE T1.DESCRIPTION = 'Body Mass Index'

prefix_hints.sol_1: User names are in `user_profiles`, while their tweets are in `tweets`, so I start from the profiles: `FROM user_profiles AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join each profile to its tweets through the shared user id: `FROM user_profiles AS T1 JOIN tweets AS T2 ON T1.uid = T2.uid`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I group the joined rows by tweet author so each group represents one user's tweets: `FROM user_profiles AS T1 JOIN tweets AS T2 ON T1.uid = T2.uid GROUP BY T2.uid`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I retain the user groups containing more than one tweet: `FROM user_profiles AS T1 JOIN tweets AS T2 ON T1.uid = T2.uid GROUP BY T2.uid HAVING count(*) > 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I project the names of those qualifying users, completing the query: `SELECT T1.name FROM user_profiles AS T1 JOIN tweets AS T2 ON T1.uid  =  T2.uid GROUP BY T2.uid HAVING count(*)  >  1`.
